thread.title: Google, Facebook, Amazon Wait To See If Congress Whiffs On Consumer Privacy | Investor's Business Daily

author: REINHARDT KRAUSE
title: Google, Facebook, Amazon Wait To See If Congress Whiffs On Consumer Privacy | Investor's Business Daily
text:
Momentum is building for federal legislation that would create stronger consumer privacy rules covering internet platforms and broadband service providers.
X And U.S. technology and telecom giants are fine with that, based on their testimony at a U.S. Senate Commerce Committee hearing this past week. Executives from Apple ( AAPL ), Amazon.com ( AMZN ), Alphabet 's ( GOOGL ) Google, AT&T ( T ) and Twitter ( TWTR ) showed support for the movement.
Europe began enforcing its General Data Protection Regulation in May, sparking a regulatory rethink of U.S. privacy protection. Tech and telecom firms prefer national legislation to state-by-state action. Some insist it be meaningful and are willing to take it to federal agencies if Congress doesn't act.
"We want the bar to be high enough on federal legislation to provide protection to the consumer that's effective," Guy Tribble, Apple's VP of software technology, said at the hearing .

In June, California passed its own consumer privacy legislation. Its rules don't take effect until 2020, giving Congress time to act on a national law that would supersede California's.
Would Federal Privacy Rules Be Watered Down? California's law grants consumers the right to know what information companies are collecting, and with whom they are sharing it. If consumers opt out, ISPs and internet firms still must provide the same quality of service.
While Apple, Google, Amazon, and AT&T may want lawmakers to pass federal legislation, it's uncertain whether Congress is up to the task. In rare bipartisan accord, the House and Senate reached a compromise on an opioid bill this week, but whether they can muster another unified effort on internet privacy is unclear.
Plus, there are political considerations with this year's midterm elections. According to polls, Democrats could grab control of the House from Republicans. A potential House-Senate split in 2019-2020 could make it tough to pass national consumer privacy laws wanted by tech and telecom giants.
Bigger Privacy Role For FTC? One question is whether the Federal Trade Commission will take on a bigger role in enforcing privacy rules if legislation stalls. The FTC plans to hold hearings on data privacy as well as antitrust and other issues this fall.
Google and Facebook ( FB ), the dominant duo in digital advertising, have the most at stake. Google and Facebook have thrived by tracking users' online and mobile activities to serve up personalized advertising.
"The FTC will want to avoid making new privacy policy just as Congress is trying to act," Cowen analyst Paul Gallant said in a recent note to clients. "But it's tricky to gauge how far the FTC will actually go — Chairman (Joseph) Simons hasn't said much on privacy, and there's no real visibility into the FTC's consent decree process."
Facebook, Google Violating Consent Decrees? The FTC is investigating Facebook's possible noncompliance with a 2012 consent decree on consumer privacy protection. The agency in 2013 ended a Google probe after the internet search giant agreed to voluntarily change its business practices. The FTC had charged that Google misrepresented to Apple mobile browser users that it would not place tracking "cookies" or serve them targeted ads.
The agency may be looking into Google's location-tracking practices. The internet search giant reportedly has stored users' locations even when consumers turn off the option on iPhones and Android devices.
"We think an FTC ruling on Facebook/Google consent decrees is likely in Q1, 2019," Gallant said.
European antitrust regulators have hit Google twice with multibillion dollar fines. In August, the European Union said Google has used its Android mobile phone operating system to bully smartphone makers. The EU last year said Google skewed search results to benefit its own shopping-search service vs. those of rivals.
Amazon Antitrust Foe At FTC Amazon, meanwhile, may have its own worries at the FTC.
Rohit Chopra, a Democratic FTC member, in July brought in a new legal assistant specialized in antitrust. Lina Khan, the legal fellow, in 2017 published a paper called "Amazon's Antitrust Paradox." Khan called for more antitrust scrutiny of the e-commerce giant.
"Despite providing immense value for consumers, new readings of antitrust law that favor a structural view rather than consumer-benefit view could bring Amazon into focus," Piper Jaffray analyst Michael Olson said in his recent note to clients. "We think precedent will be upheld but near-to-medium-term noise from the FTC may cause air-pockets for the stock."
The Trump administration, meanwhile, could issue an executive order instructing federal antitrust and law enforcement agencies to open probes into the business practices of Google, Facebook and other social media companies.
